title: Abortion & the Unborn
desc: Passages cited in discussions about personhood, life, and the status of the unborn.
overview: This topic is contested because Scripture never directly addresses elective abortion, so the debate turns on what the Bible implies about when personhood begins and how the unborn are valued. Those defending full personhood from conception point to womb-formation and prenatal-calling texts (Psalm 139, Jeremiah 1:5, Luke 1) as treating the unborn as known persons. Others note that key legal texts like Exodus 21:22-25 and Numbers 5 seem to assign the fetus a different status than a living person, and that Genesis 2:7 ties life to the first breath. The core interpretive challenge is genre: poetry and prophetic calling texts express God's intimate involvement without defining a biological threshold, while case law reflects ancient legal categories that must be read in context.
positions: Personhood at later development or birth

verses.note: God knitting a person together in the womb — widely cited for the personhood of the unborn.
God knowing and appointing Jeremiah before birth — used to argue for prenatal personhood.
John the Baptist leaping in the womb at Mary's greeting — cited for fetal awareness and personhood.
Injury to a pregnant woman — the legal status of the unborn has been debated extensively from this text.
'Sinful from conception' — cited for personhood beginning at conception.
Life begins when God breathes breath into the nostrils — cited by some as marking the start of personhood at birth.
A priest-administered test that could end a pregnancy — cited in debates about how the OT law treated fetal life.
Job cursing the day of his birth and mourning stillbirths — cited in discussions of fetal life and personhood.
The Servant called from the womb — another prenatal calling passage.
'Rescue those being led away to death' — cited in arguments about speaking for the vulnerable.
The LORD 'formed you from the womb' — another prenatal-formation text cited for God's involvement before birth.
Samson set apart as a Nazirite from the womb — cited for a person's calling and consecration beginning before birth.
'Did not he who made me in the womb make them?' — Job grounds the equal dignity of persons in shared origin in the womb.
The mystery of how the spirit and bones form in the womb — cited for the hidden, God-directed nature of prenatal life.
John 'filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb' — cited for spiritual life and personhood before birth.

title: Homosexuality
desc: Passages cited across traditions in discussions about same-sex relationships.
overview: The debate is genuinely contested because a small number of texts carry enormous weight, and their translation, cultural context, and scope are all disputed. Traditionalists read Leviticus 18:22, Romans 1:26-27, and the Corinthian and Timothy vice lists as a consistent prohibition rooted in the male-female creational design of Genesis 1-2. Affirming interpreters argue the biblical writers had no concept of a fixed sexual orientation or of covenanted same-sex partnership, and that terms like arsenokoitai and malakoi are ambiguous and may target exploitative practices. A major interpretive challenge is how to read the Sodom narrative, since Ezekiel 16 names pride and neglect of the poor rather than sexuality. The discussion also involves how ancient household and purity codes translate into modern ethics.

verses.note: Male and female created in God's image, blessed and called to multiply — cited for male-female as the created norm.
Man and woman united as one flesh — cited as the foundational definition of marriage.
Male same-sex intercourse prohibited — the primary Levitical text; context and application debated.
Paul describes same-sex relations as contrary to nature — the most discussed NT text on this topic.
A list including arsenokoitai and malakoi — translation and meaning of these terms is actively debated.
Jesus defines marriage with reference to Genesis male/female — cited for the traditional view.
The men of Sodom — whether the sin was sexual violence, inhospitality, or homosexuality specifically is debated.
Sodom's sin described as pride and neglect of the poor — cited by those who question a primarily sexual reading.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — cited in affirming arguments about the inclusivity of the new covenant.
'What God has made clean, do not call unclean' — cited in some affirming arguments about moral revision.
Arsenokoitai again listed among the lawless — the meaning of this rare term is central to the translation debate.
Angels who left their proper place and Sodom's pursuit of 'strange flesh' — cited in debates over what Sodom's sin actually was.

title: Gender Identity
desc: Passages cited in discussions about biological sex, gender, and identity.
overview: This topic is contested because the Bible speaks of a created male-female order yet also records people who fall outside expected gender categories, and it never addresses gender identity in modern terms. Traditional interpreters emphasize Genesis 1:27 and Jesus's appeal to 'male and female' as a fixed, good creational binary. Others point to eunuchs — people whose bodies and roles did not fit the binary — being explicitly welcomed (Isaiah 56, Matthew 19:12, Acts 8), and to the goodness of embodiment in Psalm 139. The interpretive challenge is cultural distance: texts like the Deuteronomy 22:5 cross-dressing prohibition arise from specific ancient contexts, and 'eunuch' covered a range of conditions that do not map cleanly onto contemporary categories.

verses.note: 'Male and female he created them' — the primary text cited for the binary nature of biological sex.
Prohibition on cross-dressing — cited in traditional arguments; applicability to gender identity is debated.
'Fearfully and wonderfully made' — cited both for the goodness of embodiment and for affirmation of gender diverse experience.
Jesus references 'male and female at the beginning' — cited for the creational norm of binary sex.
Eunuchs given 'a name better than sons and daughters' — cited in affirming arguments about gender non-conformity.
'Eunuchs born that way' — cited by some as acknowledging biological sex variations.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — cited for the diminished significance of gender distinctions in the new covenant.
'New creation' in Christ — cited in arguments about identity being redefined by the gospel.
Body as temple of the Holy Spirit — cited in discussions about the significance of the body.
The Ethiopian eunuch baptized and welcomed — cited for the full inclusion of a gender-non-conforming person.

title: Marriage & Divorce
desc: What Scripture says about the nature, purpose, and dissolution of marriage.
overview: Divorce and remarriage are contested because Jesus's sayings appear in different forms across the Gospels and interact with a first-century Jewish debate. Matthew records an exception 'for sexual immorality' (porneia), while Mark and Luke record no exception at all — raising the question of whether Matthew clarifies or softens Jesus's words. The teaching also engages the Hillel-Shammai dispute over Deuteronomy 24: whether a man could divorce for 'any cause' or only for serious offense. Paul adds a further ground (the 'Pauline privilege') when an unbelieving spouse departs. Interpreters differ on how many legitimate grounds for divorce and remarriage exist, and on whether Malachi 2:16 says God 'hates divorce' or describes the man who 'hates and divorces' — a genuine textual question.

verses.note: The first marriage — used as the template for marriage across the traditions.
Jesus on divorce: allows it for sexual immorality (πορνεία), affirms the original creational design.
Paul on marriage, celibacy, and divorce — includes the 'Pauline privilege' for mixed marriages.
Husband and wife as a picture of Christ and the church — foundational but interpretation of roles is widely debated.
'God hates divorce' — a strong statement requiring context; the exact Hebrew is also debated.
Romantic and erotic love celebrated as God's good gift within covenant relationship.
'Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure.'
Paul commends singleness as freeing one for undivided devotion to God.
The capable wife — a poem celebrating a woman of strength and dignity, not passivity.
Man and woman becoming 'one flesh' — the foundational one-flesh union Jesus appeals to against divorce.
The certificate of divorce for 'something indecent' — the text behind the Hillel/Shammai 'any cause' debate.
The exception clause 'except for sexual immorality' — central to how many grounds for divorce Jesus allowed.
Jesus on divorce with no exception clause — cited in debates over whether Matthew's exception was original.
The 'Pauline privilege' — a believer freed when an unbelieving spouse departs; a second recognized ground.

title: Slavery
desc: The Bible's complex engagement with slavery — from regulation to liberation.
overview: This topic is contested because the Bible regulates slavery rather than abolishing it outright, and the same texts have been used both to defend and to condemn it. Defenders of biblical morality distinguish the Bible's regulated servitude — with release laws, protections for runaways, and death for kidnappers — from the race-based chattel slavery of the Atlantic trade. Critics note that the law permitted permanent enslavement of foreigners (Leviticus 25:44-46) and that the New Testament instructs slaves to obey masters rather than commanding emancipation. The key interpretive challenge is trajectory: whether texts like Galatians 3:28 and Philemon plant principles that undermine slavery over time, or whether Scripture's accommodation to an ancient institution limits its moral witness.

verses.note: Hebrew slave laws — provide rights and release, but also permit certain forms of bondservitude.
'Do not return a runaway slave' — remarkable protection for escaped slaves in the ancient world.
'Enslavers' (ἀνδραποδισταῖς) listed among the lawless — cited as a condemnation of slave-trading.
Paul's letter urging Philemon to receive Onesimus as a 'dear brother' — the seed of abolition in the NT.
'Neither slave nor free in Christ' — cited as undermining slavery's fundamental premise.
Instructions to slaves and masters — cited both to justify and to critique slavery, depending on the reading.
'If you can gain your freedom, do so' — Paul encouraging slaves to seek freedom when possible.
Kidnapping someone for enslavement is punishable by death — cited against the Atlantic slave trade.
Fellow Israelites not to be treated as slaves — a principle with wider implications.
Paul asks that Onesimus be received 'no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother' — the seed of abolition.
Foreign slaves could be held as permanent property — the hardest OT text for defenders of biblical morality.
Slaves and masters addressed together, masters warned they too have a Master — cited for reciprocal accountability.
Slaves told to honor masters, especially believing ones — cited in debates over the NT's accommodation to slavery.
'You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men' — freedom in Christ reframing earthly status.
Babylon's cargo listed as ending with 'slaves, that is, human souls' — cited as an indictment of the slave trade.

title: End Times & Eschatology
desc: Passages central to the major views on what happens at the end of history.
overview: End-times interpretation is contested because apocalyptic and prophetic texts use symbolic imagery that can be read literally or figuratively, and because Jesus's timing statements are hard to place. The main millennial positions — premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism — read Revelation 20's thousand years very differently, as a future earthly reign, a present growing age, or a symbolic period. Preterists argue much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation were fulfilled in AD 70, while futurists see them as still to come. Rapture debates (pre-, mid-, post-tribulation) hinge largely on a single passage, 1 Thessalonians 4. The central challenge is genre: knowing when apocalyptic language is a coded description of real events and when it is symbolic theology.

verses.note: The Olivet Discourse — Jesus's teaching on the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the age; fulfilled vs. future readings debated.
The 'rapture' passage — believers caught up to meet the Lord; pre/mid/post-tribulation debates center here.
The thousand-year reign — the key text dividing pre-, post-, and amillennialists.
The 70 weeks — one of the most interpreted prophetic passages; various 'gap' and 'no gap' readings exist.
The Day of the LORD and the new heavens and earth — annihilation or renewal of the cosmos?
The new creation — wolves and lambs together; cited by premillennialists for a literal future kingdom.
'He will come back in the same way you have seen him go' — the bodily return of Christ.
Apocalyptic battle at Jerusalem — interpreted literally by some, symbolically by others.
'Some standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming' — fuels preterist readings.
New Jerusalem descending from heaven — the goal of all history; God dwells with humanity.
'This generation will not pass away' — the key text for preterist vs. futurist readings of the Olivet Discourse.
Believers 'caught up' to meet the Lord — the one explicit rapture text where pre/mid/post-trib debates center.
'The day of the Lord will come like a thief' with the elements dissolved — cited in cosmos-renewal vs. destruction debates.
'Will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?' — cited on whether a national/earthly kingdom is still expected.
'The fullness of the Gentiles' and 'all Israel will be saved' — key to debates over Israel's future in God's plan.

title: Predestination & Free Will
desc: The great debate between divine sovereignty and human responsibility.
overview: This is the classic tension between God's sovereign choice and human freedom, and it is contested because Scripture strongly affirms both. Calvinists read election texts (Romans 8-9, Ephesians 1, John 6, Acts 13:48) as teaching that God unconditionally chooses who will be saved and effectually draws them. Arminians and others emphasize texts of universal saving desire and open invitation (2 Peter 3:9, 1 Timothy 2:4, Ezekiel 18, Revelation 22:17), arguing election is conditioned on foreseen faith or is corporate rather than individual. The interpretive challenge is holding together God's initiative and genuine human responsibility, and deciding whether Romans 9 concerns individual salvation or God's freedom in redemptive history.

verses.note: 'Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified' — the golden chain of Calvinist soteriology.
Chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world — foundational for Reformed election theology.
'No one can come to me unless the Father draws them' — cited for unconditional election.
Jacob and Esau, the potter and clay — Paul's strongest argument for God's sovereign choice.
'As many as were appointed to eternal life believed' — a key Calvinist proof text.
God is 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' — central to Arminian arguments.
'Whoever believes' — the open invitation of the gospel cited for human responsibility.
God desires all people to be saved — cited for universal salvific will.
'Let the one who desires take the water of life without price' — the open invitation.
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked — cited for genuine divine desire for all to turn.
Jacob and Esau and the potter and clay — Paul's strongest statement of God's sovereign, unconditional choice.
'All that the Father gives me will come to me' — cited for effectual, unconditional drawing to Christ.
God 'desires all people to be saved' — central to arguments for a universal saving will.

title: Hell & Eternal Punishment
desc: Passages addressing the nature, duration, and reality of hell and final judgment.
overview: The debate centers on whether hell involves eternal conscious torment, the annihilation of the wicked, or the eventual restoration of all. The eternal conscious torment view (held by most of church history) reads texts like Revelation 20 and Matthew 25:46 as describing unending suffering. Annihilationists (or conditionalists) argue that 'eternal' describes the finality of destruction rather than duration of suffering, and that only God possesses inherent immortality. Universalists point to texts like Colossians 1:20 and Romans 11:32 to argue that God's redemptive purposes ultimately encompass all. The word 'Gehenna' — Jesus's most common term — referred to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, used for burning refuse and associated with Josiah's defilement of child sacrifice sites.

verses.note: 'Eternal fire' and 'eternal punishment' vs. 'eternal life' — the parallel between the two is central to the torment view.
The lake of fire, 'tormented day and night forever,' and the 'second death' — the strongest eternal-torment text.
Gehenna 'where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' — Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning garbage valley.
'Eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord' — cited by annihilationists for destruction, by others for separation.
'The wages of sin is death' — annihilationists read 'death' as cessation of existence, contrasted with the gift of eternal life.
Fear the one who can 'destroy both soul and body in hell' — the word 'destroy' (apollumi) is central to the annihilation debate.
Sodom as an example of 'eternal fire' — yet Sodom was destroyed, not eternally burning, cited by annihilationists.
The undying worm and unquenched fire over the corpses of rebels — the source of Jesus's Gehenna imagery.
'The smoke of their torment goes up forever' — cited for unending conscious suffering.
God 'alone has immortality' — cited by conditionalists arguing humans are not inherently immortal.
'Should not perish but have eternal life' — the meaning of 'perish' (apollumi) is disputed between the views.
Christ remaining in heaven 'until the restoration of all things' — a key universalist text.
God reconciling 'all things to himself' through Christ — cited by universalists for cosmic reconciliation.
'In Christ all shall be made alive' and God 'all in all' — a leading universalist passage.
'Every knee shall bow... every tongue confess' — whether willingly or under compulsion is the interpretive crux.
The rich man and Lazarus — flame, torment, and a fixed 'great chasm' in Hades; a parable's literal weight is debated.
Resurrection to 'everlasting life' or to 'shame and everlasting contempt' — an early two-destinies text.

title: Water Baptism
desc: The mode, meaning, and necessity of baptism across Christian traditions.
overview: Baptism is contested over three questions: its meaning, its proper recipients, and its mode. Baptismal-regeneration traditions read Acts 2:38, 1 Peter 3:21, and Titus 3:5 as teaching that baptism actually conveys forgiveness and new birth. Most Protestants treat it as a symbol or sign of a salvation already received by faith, citing the thief on the cross and the Spirit falling on Cornelius before baptism. Credobaptists limit baptism to professing believers, while paedobaptists baptize infants, linking baptism to circumcision as a covenant sign (Colossians 2:11-12). The interpretive challenge is that the New Testament describes adult-convert baptisms without directly settling the infant question, and its language about baptism 'saving' must be weighed against salvation by grace through faith.

verses.note: 'Go and baptize' — the command foundational to all traditions of Christian baptism.
'Repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins' — cited for baptismal regeneration.
Baptism as dying and rising with Christ — the participatory/symbolic meaning.
'Baptism now saves you' — one of the strongest baptismal regeneration texts; the parenthetical context is disputed.
'Clothed with Christ through baptism' — union with Christ through the rite.
The Spirit falls before baptism — cited by those who see baptism as a response to grace, not its vehicle.
The thief on the cross promised paradise without baptism — cited against baptism as strictly necessary.
Baptism linked to circumcision — a key text for paedobaptists (infant baptism).
John's water baptism contrasted with the Spirit baptism Jesus brings — raises questions about the two.
'Buried with him in baptism' and raised through faith — key text linking baptism, burial, and paedobaptist covenant logic.
'Instruction about baptisms' (plural) among elementary doctrines — cited in debates over how many baptisms there are.

title: Baptism in the Holy Spirit
desc: What Spirit-baptism is, when it occurs, and whether tongues are its evidence.
overview: This topic is contested because Acts records the Spirit coming in several different sequences, and traditions disagree on whether Spirit-baptism is part of conversion or a distinct later empowering. Pentecostals and many charismatics see a 'second blessing' subsequent to conversion, often evidenced by speaking in tongues, drawing on the Samaritan, Cornelius, and Ephesian accounts. Cessationists and many Reformed readers take 1 Corinthians 12:13 to mean all believers are baptized in the Spirit at conversion, and view the Acts patterns as unrepeatable transitional events. The interpretive challenge is whether the narratives of Acts are meant to establish a normative pattern or simply describe how the Spirit spread to distinct groups (Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles, disciples of John).

verses.note: Jesus commands the disciples to wait for the baptism of the Holy Spirit — the initiating promise.
Pentecost — the Spirit poured out with tongues of fire; tongues as first sign.
The 'Gentile Pentecost' — Spirit falls on Cornelius's household with tongues before water baptism.
Samaritans receive the Spirit through the laying on of hands — a distinct second experience.
Ephesian disciples rebaptized and Spirit received with tongues and prophecy.
'By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body' — cited by those who see Spirit-baptism as conversion.
Tongues as prayer and edification — Paul's nuanced treatment of the gift.
'Rivers of living water' — referring to the Spirit not yet given; anticipates Pentecost.
'How much more will your Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask' — ongoing prayer for the Spirit.
Ephesian disciples receive the Spirit with tongues and prophecy after Paul lays hands on them — a subsequent experience.
All were 'filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues' — cited for tongues as initial evidence.
Praying and singing 'with my spirit' in tongues — cited for tongues as a personal prayer language.
Jesus breathed on the disciples: 'Receive the Holy Spirit' — debated as distinct from or anticipating Pentecost.

title: Sabbath Rest
desc: Whether Christians are bound to the Sabbath, and what rest means in Christ.
overview: The Sabbath question is contested because it is the one Ten Commandments law whose ongoing obligation Christians dispute. Sabbatarians ground it in creation (Genesis 2) and the moral law (Exodus 20), arguing it remains binding, whether on Saturday or transferred to Sunday. Others hold it was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17) and now a matter of freedom (Romans 14:5-6), pointing out that Deuteronomy 5 roots the command in the exodus rather than creation. A further view finds the Sabbath's true meaning in the ongoing rest of faith described in Hebrews 4. The challenge is distinguishing moral, ceremonial, and covenantal dimensions of the command, and reading Jesus's Sabbath sayings, which both honor and relativize the institution.

verses.note: God rests on the seventh day and hallows it — the creational foundation of Sabbath.
The fourth commandment — Sabbath as covenant sign; its continuing applicability is debated.
'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' — Jesus relativizes the Sabbath institution.
Sabbath described as a 'shadow' of what was to come; its observance not required — key text for fulfilled-Sabbath view.
Each person should be 'fully convinced in their own mind' about observing days.
A 'Sabbath rest remains for the people of God' — interpreted as rest in Christ or a literal future rest.
The church meeting on the first day of the week — the basis for Sunday as the Christian gathering day.
Sabbath as delight, not burden — God's vision of joyful rest.
'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath' — Jesus's authority over the institution.
The Sabbath command grounded in the exodus, not creation — cited in debates over the Sabbath's basis and permanence.
'All flesh' worshiping from Sabbath to Sabbath in the new creation — cited for the Sabbath's abiding significance.

title: Tithing & Giving
desc: Whether the tithe is a binding Christian obligation or a guide for generous giving.
overview: Tithing is contested over whether the Old Testament tenth is binding on Christians or whether the New Testament replaces it with freewill, proportional generosity. Advocates of the tithe cite Abraham and Jacob tithing before the Law, Jesus affirming the tithe in Matthew 23:23, and Malachi 3:10's storehouse command. Others argue the tithe was part of Israel's covenant economy that actually funded Levites, festivals, and the poor, and that the New Testament nowhere commands a tithe but calls for cheerful, sacrificial, sometimes far greater giving. The interpretive challenge is that Israel arguably had multiple tithes serving different purposes, so mapping a single 10 percent rule onto the church requires care.

verses.note: 'Bring the full tithe into the storehouse' — the most-quoted tithing text; context is OT covenant.
Abraham tithing to Melchizedek before the Mosaic law — cited for tithing as a pre-law principle.
Jesus commends tithing 'mint and dill' while not neglecting justice and mercy — affirmation of tithing in principle.
'Give what you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion' — cited against mandatory tithing.
Melchizedek's tithe shows the superiority of Melchizedek's priesthood — used to argue for tithing in the new covenant.
The widow's offering — Jesus commends sacrificial giving beyond a mere percentage.
Regular proportional giving on the first day of the week — the NT giving principle.
Early church sharing everything — a model of radical generosity beyond the tithe.
'A tenth of everything from the land belongs to the LORD' — the Mosaic tithe's original context.
Abram gives Melchizedek 'a tenth of everything' before the Law — cited for tithing as a pre-Mosaic principle.
Jacob vows to give God a tenth — a second pre-Law example cited by tithe advocates.
The tithe given to the Levites for their service — shows the tithe's covenant purpose in Israel's economy.
A tithe eaten in celebration before God and shared with the poor and Levite — evidence of more than one tithe.

title: Church Leadership
desc: Who may lead, how authority works, and the shape of healthy church governance.
overview: Church leadership is contested over both structure and eligibility. Traditions differ on polity — episcopal (bishops), presbyterian (a body of elders), and congregational (local church authority) — and on whether the New Testament prescribes a single model or leaves it flexible. There is also debate over titles and offices: whether 'elder,' 'overseer,' and 'pastor' name one office or several, and how the fivefold ministry of Ephesians 4 relates to elders and deacons. Underlying all of it is the servant-leadership ethic Jesus taught, which reframes authority as service. The interpretive challenge is that the texts give qualifications and snapshots of practice rather than a comprehensive governance manual.

verses.note: Qualifications for overseers and deacons — the most detailed NT leadership criteria.
Elder qualifications for local churches — parallel to 1 Timothy 3; character-centred.
Elders to 'shepherd the flock' as undershepherds under Christ; servant leadership, not dominance.
Jesus defines greatness as servanthood — the counter-cultural leadership model.
Paul appointing elders in every church — plurality of elders as the Pauline pattern.
'I do not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man' — central to complementarian arguments.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — central to egalitarian arguments about leadership.
Phoebe as διάκονος (deacon/minister) — evidence of women in formal church roles.
Junia 'outstanding among the apostles' — debated: was Junia an apostle, or notable to the apostles?
Priscilla (listed first) explains the way of God to Apollos — a woman teaching a man in Acts.
Seven chosen to serve tables so the apostles could focus on word and prayer — often read as the origin of deacons.
'Obey your leaders and submit to them' — cited for the real authority church leaders hold.
Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers given to equip the saints — the 'fivefold ministry' text.
The sick to 'call the elders of the church' to pray — assumes a recognized body of elders in each congregation.

title: Divine Healing
desc: Whether miraculous healing is in the atonement, promised for today, and how to pray for the sick.
overview: Divine healing is contested over whether physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement and normative for today. Word-of-faith and many Pentecostal teachers read Isaiah 53 and its Gospel application (Matthew 8:16-17) as securing bodily healing alongside forgiveness, so that healing can be claimed by faith. Others hold that Isaiah 53 primarily concerns healing from sin (as 1 Peter 2:24 applies it), that healing is a gift distributed as the Spirit wills, and that God does not always heal — citing Paul's unremoved thorn and sick companions. Cessationists further argue the miraculous gifts served to authenticate the apostolic era. The interpretive challenge is holding genuine expectation of God's power together with the biblical reality of unhealed, faithful believers.

verses.note: 'By his stripes we are healed' — cited for healing in the atonement; Matthew applies it to Jesus's healing ministry.
Jesus heals all who are sick to 'fulfill what was spoken by Isaiah the prophet' — Matthew's application of Isaiah 53.
'Is any among you sick? Let the elders pray' — the primary NT text for healing prayer.
'By his wounds you have been healed' — Peter quotes Isaiah 53 in the context of spiritual healing (from sin).
Signs including healing will follow believers — the longer ending; text-critical issues noted.
Paul's thorn was not healed despite three prayers — cited to balance triumphalist healing theology.
Paul advises Timothy to take wine for his stomach — medical means not excluded by faith.
Epaphroditus nearly died — illness is not always rebuked or immediately healed.
Man blind from birth — Jesus says it was not due to sin; corrects the equation of suffering with faithlessness.
Peter heals the lame man 'in the name of Jesus Christ' — a model apostolic healing in Acts.
'Gifts of healing' listed among the Spirit's gifts — cited for healing as a distributed gift, not a universal guarantee.
'Trophimus I left ill at Miletus' — Paul does not heal a coworker, cited to temper guaranteed-healing claims.
Epaphroditus 'was ill, near to death' — a devoted believer whose illness was real and prolonged.

title: Women in Ministry
desc: A central debate: may women preach, teach, and lead in the church?
overview: This is the central complementarian-egalitarian debate: whether women may teach and hold authoritative leadership over men in the church. Complementarians read 1 Timothy 2:11-12 and 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 as permanent restrictions grounded in creation order, reserving eldership and authoritative teaching for men. Egalitarians read those texts as addressing specific local problems and point to women who prophesied, taught, and led — Deborah, Priscilla, Phoebe, and possibly the apostle Junia — alongside Galatians 3:28 and the Spirit poured out on 'sons and daughters.' The interpretive challenge is weighing a few restrictive texts against many examples of women in ministry, and deciding which instructions are culturally bound and which are transcultural.

verses.note: 'Neither male nor female — all are one in Christ Jesus' — the foundational egalitarian text.
Paul does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man — the foundational complementarian text.
Women to be silent in churches — context (asking questions vs. all speech) and application are debated.
Women praying and prophesying in church — assumes women speak publicly, just with head covered.
'Your daughters will prophesy' — the Spirit's outpouring explicitly includes women as proclaimers.
Philip's four daughters were prophetesses — acknowledged female prophetic ministry.
Phoebe commended as a deacon and benefactor — evidence of a woman in formal church ministry.
Deborah as both prophet and judge of all Israel — a woman exercising the highest leadership in the OT.
The capable woman 'speaks with wisdom' and teaches — wisdom as a feminine voice in Proverbs.
Male and female together given dominion — cited for shared authority rooted in creation.
Junia 'outstanding among the apostles' — whether Junia was a female apostle is a pivotal contested point.
'I do not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man' — the central complementarian text, its scope debated.

title: Capital Punishment
desc: Biblical teaching on whether the state may lawfully take a life as punishment.
overview: Capital punishment is contested over whether the biblical warrant for the death penalty still applies under the new covenant. Supporters cite Genesis 9:6, given before the Law and grounded in the image of God, and Romans 13:4, where the governing authority 'bears the sword,' as ongoing divine sanction. Opponents point to Jesus's revision of 'eye for eye,' his refusal to condemn the woman caught in adultery, and the priority of mercy and the sanctity of life, arguing the state should not take life. A key interpretive challenge is distinguishing the civil penalties of Israel's covenant law from principles binding on all nations, and discerning how Jesus's teaching reshapes Old Testament justice.

verses.note: 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed' — the foundational text for capital punishment.
Death for murder in Mosaic law — intentional vs. unintentional distinctions.
Government 'does not bear the sword in vain' — widely cited for state authority to execute.
No ransom accepted for murder — the death penalty is mandatory in the Mosaic system.
The woman caught in adultery — Jesus does not enforce the death penalty; cited for its abolition.
'You have heard eye for eye…but I say turn the other cheek' — Jesus's revision of retributive justice.
'Vengeance is mine, says the Lord' — cited for entrusting justice to God rather than human execution.
Paul acknowledges that if he deserves death, he will not resist it — implicit affirmation of the state's right.
Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent are both abominations to God.
A list of capital offenses in the Mosaic law — cited in debates over which penalties were covenant-specific.
Jesus traces murder back to anger in the heart — cited for a deeper, mercy-oriented reading of the law.
'If anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword he must be slain' — cited on divine justice and human violence.
'The soul who sins shall die' — cited for individual moral accountability before God.

title: Just War & Pacifism
desc: May a Christian fight? When, if ever, is war justifiable?
overview: Whether a Christian may take up arms is contested because the Bible both portrays God as a warrior and calls his people to peacemaking and enemy-love. Just-war advocates cite the state's God-given sword (Romans 13), John the Baptist's failure to tell soldiers to quit, and the devout centurion Cornelius, arguing force can restrain evil under proper limits. Pacifists center Jesus's Sermon on the Mount — 'turn the other cheek,' 'blessed are the peacemakers' — and his refusal of the sword, holding that his followers renounce lethal violence. The interpretive challenge is reconciling the militant imagery of the Old Testament and Revelation with Jesus's nonviolent example, and deciding whether his commands govern personal conduct, the church, or the state as well.

verses.note: Governing authorities bear the sword against evil — the primary text for Christian participation in state force.
'Blessed are the peacemakers' — the beatitude foundational to pacifist ethics.
'Do not resist the evil person' — the non-resistance command at the heart of pacifism.
Soldiers told to be content with their pay, not to quit the army — John the Baptist does not condemn military service.
'Greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends' — cited for soldiers' sacrifice.
'They will beat their swords into plowshares' — the eschatological vision of universal peace.
'A time for war and a time for peace' — cited for the legitimacy of war in a fallen world.
Jesus tells the disciples to buy swords — variously interpreted as literal, symbolic, or a limited provision.
Christ himself returns as a warrior king — cited for just-war theology's divine legitimacy.
'The LORD is a man of war' — cited for the legitimacy of righteous warfare in the Old Testament.
God 'makes wars cease to the end of the earth' — cited for God's ultimate purpose of peace.
'Turn the other cheek' and 'love your enemies' — the heart of the pacifist case.
'My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would fight' — cited on the church renouncing the sword.
Cornelius, a 'devout' centurion, commended and never told to leave the army — cited for compatible military service.
Submit to governing authorities who punish evildoers — cited for the legitimacy of state force.

title: Alcohol & Sobriety
desc: From wine at Cana to warnings about drunkenness — what the Bible says about drinking.
overview: Christians disagree over whether Scripture permits moderate drinking or calls for total abstinence. Moderationists point to wine as a gift that 'gladdens the heart,' Jesus making wine at Cana, Paul prescribing wine for Timothy's stomach, and the condemnation being reserved for drunkenness, not drinking. Abstentionists emphasize the many warnings against alcohol, the Nazirite vow, concern for weaker believers (Romans 14), and the wisdom of avoiding a substance linked to so much harm. A prohibitionist minority argues the 'wine' commended was unfermented. The interpretive challenge is distinguishing descriptive from prescriptive texts and weighing Christian liberty against love that limits freedom for the sake of others.

verses.note: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding — and the headwaiter praises its quality; cited for moderate drinking.
'Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler' — a strong warning against alcohol's dangers.
'Do not get drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit' — the NT's clearest prohibition of drunkenness.
Paul tells Timothy to drink a little wine for his stomach — medicinal use of wine affirmed.
'Give wine to those who are bitter in soul' — wine as comfort for the suffering; not absolute prohibition.
It is good not to drink wine if it causes a brother to stumble — conscience and community over personal freedom.
The Nazirite vow requires abstaining from all wine — total abstinence as a form of holy consecration.
Drunkenness listed among the works of the flesh that exclude from God's kingdom.
'Wine that gladdens human hearts' — creation's gift; God's good provision for joy.
'Wine to gladden the heart of man' — cited for wine as part of God's good creation.
Woe to those who 'run after strong drink' from morning on — a strong warning against alcohol's grip.

title: Wealth & Poverty
desc: Does God promise prosperity? How should Christians relate to money?
overview: Scripture's treatment of money is contested because it both blesses prosperity and issues severe warnings about riches. Prosperity teaching reads covenant blessings and generosity promises as guaranteeing material increase to the faithful. Others hold that wealth is a stewardship and a spiritual danger, citing Jesus's warnings, the rich fool, and 'you cannot serve God and money,' and stressing God's special concern for the poor through gleaning laws, Jubilee, and the sharing of the early church. The interpretive challenge is holding together texts that treat wealth as a blessing, as a trust, and as a snare — and discerning which economic instructions were covenant-specific and which express enduring principles of justice and generosity.
positions: Radical simplicity / preferential option for the poor

verses.note: 'Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom' — Jesus's radical warning.
'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' — not money itself, but love of it.
The rich fool who stored up earthly goods but was not rich toward God.
Rich man and Lazarus — the reversal of fortune after death; a warning against indifference to the poor.
'Weep and howl, you rich people' — James's most severe address to the wealthy who exploit workers.
'Lazy hands make for poverty' — work and diligence as paths to provision.
'God loves a cheerful giver' and will make grace abound for generous giving.
The early church held everything in common and distributed to any who had need.
'Do not say to yourself, my power produced this wealth' — God gives the ability to produce wealth.
'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD' — generosity to the poor is generosity to God.
'Give me neither poverty nor riches' — a prayer for enough, cited against both destitution and excess.
'There will be no poor among you'... 'open wide your hand' — the tension of Israel's economic ideal and command.
Gleaning laws leaving harvest edges for the poor and the sojourner — structural care for the needy.
'Lay up treasures in heaven' — cited for reorienting from material to eternal wealth.
'You cannot serve God and money' — the sharp choice Jesus sets between two masters.
Laodicea: 'I am rich... not knowing that you are wretched' — spiritual poverty masked by material wealth.
